profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting at a university-affiliated research lab preparing a cross-disciplinary graduate seminar built around The Oxford Handbook of Affective Computing. The team is reviewing the current course design proposal for a 12-week seminar that will be co-listed across computer science and psychology. The agenda is to evaluate whether the syllabus, weekly activities, and assessment structure are ready to send to the curriculum committee and invited guest lecturers. The expected outcome is agreement on whether the course design is 'ready for circulation' and what small revisions, if any, should be made before sharing it externally.

members.name: Dr. Maya Chen
members.role: Faculty lead for the seminar and affective computing researcher
members.expertise: Affective computing, multimodal sensing, research methods, graduate curriculum design
members.background: Maya is a computer science professor who runs a lab on emotion-aware interactive systems and has previously taught project-based seminars for engineering students with external industry guests.
members.private_state: She wants the seminar approved quickly so guest speakers can be confirmed, and she is trying to keep the design lightweight enough that visiting lecturers and mixed-background students will not be overwhelmed.
hidden_assumptions: If a week is marked with one 'anchor chapter,' students can selectively draw on other chapters as optional background rather than being expected to read a whole section.
'Methods coverage' in a seminar means students are exposed to methodological tradeoffs through discussion, not that they practice every method hands-on.
A design is 'ready for circulation' once the intellectual arc, weekly topics, and assignment shells are stable, even if operational details like rubrics and TA instructions are still to be filled in.
The listed 'final project' can remain at the proposal stage because seminar courses often culminate in research design memos rather than implemented systems.

members.name: Dr. Samuel Ortiz
members.role: Co-instructor from psychology and curriculum committee liaison
members.expertise: Emotion theory, experimental psychology, graduate pedagogy, program review
members.background: Samuel is an associate professor in psychology who has helped shepherd several interdisciplinary courses through committee review and often focuses on pedagogical coherence and assessment transparency.
members.private_state: He wants the course to look fully defensible to the curriculum committee and accessible to psychology students, and he is especially concerned about anything that could appear underspecified once the document leaves the instructors' hands.
hidden_assumptions: If the syllabus says a section is 'covered,' students should have required exposure to its central chapters rather than only optional mention during discussion.
'Methods coverage' implies students will concretely engage with representative techniques, artifacts, or mini-exercises so the course does not read as purely conceptual.
A design is only 'ready for circulation' when outside reviewers could evaluate grading logic, workload, and learning outcomes without needing verbal explanation from the instructors.
A 'final project' in a graduate design-oriented seminar normally includes at least a small executable prototype, analysis plan, or pilot study artifact rather than only a proposal.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as covering the handbook's methods section
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say the course 'covers the methodologies section well.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the syllabus includes one dedicated week on methodologies plus method-related discussion woven into other weeks, which is sufficient exposure for a survey seminar.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means students will have required, explicit engagement with several core methodological topics from Section Four, such as data collection, emotion representation, crowdsourcing, machine learning, and ethics, in a way visible in the written syllabus.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are reviewing a broad handbook and naturally use high-level coverage language; because neither expects to enumerate all subsection topics in conversation, the phrase sounds complete and unproblematic.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree the design should be 'ready for circulation by Friday.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means ready to email to guest lecturers and a few trusted colleagues as a near-final draft for soft feedback, with some rubric and logistics details still pending.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means ready to send as the formal packet to the curriculum committee, where it should already include polished assessment criteria, workload estimates, and complete learning outcomes.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In academic course planning, 'circulation' is a routine shorthand and both parties regularly send documents around; each assumes the intended audience is obvious from prior process context, so the ambiguity hides behind familiar workflow language.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to the 'final project' as the capstone element that ties the seminar together.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the final project is a research or design proposal for an affective computing system or study, possibly with mockups and critique, appropriate for students from mixed technical backgrounds.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the final project includes some concrete implementation, pilot data collection plan, or evaluable artifact so students demonstrate applied competence beyond proposing ideas.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Graduate seminars often use the same term for very different capstones, and both versions seem pedagogically plausible; because they are focused on reviewing the overall design rather than debating assignment details, the scope difference remains latent.

misalignment_points.topic: Which document version is 'the current draft'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both mention 'the current draft' and 'the week-by-week table' as if they are talking about the same proposal.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the updated shared document revised yesterday, where weekly readings were condensed to one anchor chapter and optional companions.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the PDF attached to last week's committee-prep email, which still lists two required chapters for several weeks and a prototype-oriented project description.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The two versions have the same title and very similar structure, and in a design review both participants assume the latest familiar file is the common reference; the overlap is large enough that early discussion feels aligned.

turns.inner_thought: I mainly need to get this stable enough to email guest speakers and a couple of trusted colleagues by Friday so I can lock people in. The shared doc I revised yesterday is in good shape: one anchor chapter per week, optional companion readings, and the overall arc is clear. I don't want us bogged down in rubric details today.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I mostly want to confirm that the design is ready for circulation by Friday, and then do a quick pass on the current draft, especially the week-by-week table.

turns.inner_thought: If we're talking about the committee-prep PDF from last week, the sequence is already persuasive: foundations, sensing, generation, methodologies, applications. It reads like a coherent interdisciplinary course. I still need the packet to be defensible as a formal submission, but the intellectual arc is there.
turns.utterance: Yes, absolutely. At a high level, I think the current draft is in strong shape. The arc moves nicely from theory into detection, generation, methodologies, and then applications, so the week-by-week table already feels coherent.

turns.inner_thought: Good, he seems comfortable with the revised structure. The one-anchor-chapter approach is exactly what this group needs; otherwise the psychology students and the engineers will both feel swamped. They can dip into other chapters as background when useful, but the visible commitment each week should stay light.
turns.utterance: Great. I intentionally streamlined each week around an anchor chapter so students coming from different backgrounds aren't overloaded, while they still get the breadth of the handbook through the overall sequence.

turns.inner_thought: I'm relieved the methodologies section is covered well in the syllabus, because committee reviewers always look for that in a cross-listed course. As long as the written document clearly shows students are engaging with the central methods material, it should satisfy the rigor question.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I'm especially glad the course covers the methodologies section well, because that's often where reviewers look when they're judging interdisciplinary rigor.

turns.inner_thought: One dedicated methods week plus methods themes woven into discussion is plenty for a seminar. Students will encounter ethics, representation choices, and data concerns in multiple places even if we don't require every subsection as a full reading block. That's enough exposure for what this course is trying to be.
turns.utterance: Right, and I think that piece lands well because the methods week does a lot of the work, and then students keep running into issues like ethics, representation, and data in the surrounding discussion weeks too.

turns.inner_thought: If the final project stays as the capstone, that should reassure reviewers that students do more than discuss concepts—they'll have to show some applied engagement through something concrete. That helps support the claim that the methods material isn't just theoretical.
turns.utterance: Yes, that tracks for me. And the final project should help demonstrate that students can actually work with those ideas rather than only talk about them.

turns.inner_thought: Exactly—the capstone is where they synthesize by proposing an affective computing system or study in a chosen domain, maybe with mockups or a design memo. For a mixed-background seminar, a strong proposal is the right level of ambition. He seems aligned on the final project, which is reassuring.
turns.utterance: I agree. The final project should nicely tie the seminar together by having students formulate an affective computing study or system concept grounded in one application area.

turns.inner_thought: In the version I'm looking at, the milestones already make the deliverables legible for committee review, especially around the project. If those remain, the packet will look sufficiently specified when it goes forward. That's another reason I think we're close to ready for circulation by Friday.
turns.utterance: One thing I like is that the week-by-week table already signals the deliverables clearly enough for external review, especially if the project milestones stay in place.

turns.inner_thought: I can polish the language a little, but I don't want to reopen the structure. Once I clean up the guest-speaker notes and reading annotations in the shared document, it's ready to send around informally. Rubrics and TA-facing logistics can come after we get initial reactions.
turns.utterance: I can still tighten the wording a bit, but from my perspective the design is basically ready for circulation once the guest speaker notes and reading annotations are cleaned up.

turns.inner_thought: Good. I just need to make sure that when this goes to the committee on Friday, the packet includes the standard assessment language—grading logic, workload, learning outcomes, the usual things reviewers expect to see without us in the room to explain. If that's there, I can stand behind it.
turns.utterance: Great. Then when it goes out on Friday, let's make sure the packet includes the usual assessment language so reviewers can see the course is fully specified.

turns.inner_thought: Sure, I can make a few surface edits and preserve the main design. I'll send the revised shared doc around at the end of the week to the guest speakers and a small circle for feedback. He sounds satisfied, so we shouldn't need a major rewrite.
turns.utterance: Absolutely. I'll make the small edits, keep the broad structure intact, and send the current draft around at the end of the week.

turns.inner_thought: Once those final packet details are in place, this should read to committee as a coherent, well-covered interdisciplinary seminar with solid methods exposure and a credible capstone. I think we're in a good position if Friday is the submission point.
turns.utterance: Perfect. Once those edits are in, I think the course will present as a coherent and well-covered interdisciplinary seminar.
